a1-verb-to-be.s: Use am, is, and are to talk about identity, feelings, and basic facts.
ex: I **am** a student.
He **is** calm today.
They **are** in the kitchen.
**Is** this your phone?

a1-subject-pronouns.t: Subject Pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they)
a1-subject-pronouns.s: Use subject pronouns as the subject of a sentence.
ex: **I** am busy today.
**You** are in the wrong room.
**He** is my brother.
**She** is a doctor.

a1-object-pronouns.t: Object Pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them)
a1-object-pronouns.s: Use object pronouns after verbs and prepositions.
ex: Can you help **me**?
I like **you**.
She knows **him** well.
We can meet **her** at 6.

a1-possessive-adjectives.t: Possessive Adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their)
a1-possessive-adjectives.s: Use possessive adjectives before nouns to show ownership.
ex: This is **my** key.
Is that **your** jacket?
**His** name is Omar.
**Her** phone is on the sofa.

a1-demonstratives.s: Use demonstratives to point to things and people.
ex: **This** is my ticket.
**That** is a great photo.
**These** are my friends.
**Those** are not my keys.

a1-a-an.s: Use a/an for one non-specific countable thing.
ex: I need **a** taxi.
She has **an** idea.
He is **a** teacher.
Can I borrow **a** pen?

a1-the-basic.s: Use the for a specific thing you and the listener know.
ex: I opened **the** window.
Where is **the** station?
I saw a dog. **The** dog was friendly.
Put **the** milk in the fridge.

a1-plural-nouns.s: Make nouns plural to talk about more than one.
ex: I have three **books**.
Two **buses** are late.
These **cities** are busy.
My **children** are at school.

a1-there-is-are.s: Use there is/are to say something exists or is present.
ex: **There is** a supermarket on this street.
**There are** two windows in the room.
**Is there** a bank near here?
**There isn't** any sugar.

a1-have-got.s: Use have got to talk about what you own or what you have.
ex: I've **got** a spare charger.
She has **got** a small car.
He hasn't **got** any cash.
Have you **got** a minute?

a1-possessive-pronouns.s: Use possessive pronouns to show ownership without repeating a noun.
ex: This seat is **mine**.
Is this umbrella **yours**?
That red bike is **hers**.
Our office is smaller than **theirs**.

a1-present-simple-affirmative.s: Use the present simple to talk about routines, facts, and repeated actions.
ex: I **start** work at 8.
She **drinks** tea every morning.
We **live** in a small flat.
My brother **plays** football on Sundays.

a1-present-simple-negatives-questions.s: Use do and does to make present simple negatives and questions.
ex: I **don't eat** breakfast early.
**Does** she **work** from home?
We **don't watch** much TV.
**Do** you **need** this cable?

a1-imperative.s: Use the imperative to give instructions, directions, and simple orders.
ex: **Open** the app and sign in.
Please **close** the door.
**Turn** left after the bridge.
**Don't run** in the corridor.

a1-can-ability-permission.s: Use can to talk about ability and to ask for or give permission.
ex: She **can** speak Spanish.
**Can** I open the window?
We **can't** come tonight.
My son **can** ride a bike now.

a1-question-words.t: Question Words (who, what, where, when, why, how)
a1-question-words.s: Use question words to ask for specific information.
ex: **Who** is your teacher?
**What** do you need?
**Where** are my glasses?
**When** does the film start?

a1-prepositions-of-place.s: Use basic place prepositions to show position and location.
ex: My coat is **on** the chair.
The milk is **in** the fridge.
The cat is **under** the bed.
She sat **next to** me on the bus.

a1-prepositions-of-time-basic.s: Use in, on, and at with common time expressions.
ex: My birthday is **in** July.
We moved here **in** 2022.
She works **on** Fridays.
The concert is **on** 14 June.

a1-some-any-basic.s: Use some and any with plural and uncountable nouns in simple statements and questions.
ex: There are **some** clean towels upstairs.
I need **some** help with this form.
We don't have **any** bread.
Are there **any** seats left?

a1-numbers-dates-time.t: Numbers, Dates, and Telling the Time
a1-numbers-dates-time.s: Use basic number and time patterns to talk about dates, prices, ages, and schedules.
ex: It is **half past** seven.
My appointment is **at 10:15**.
Her birthday is **on 4 September**.
The room is on the **third** floor.

a1-basic-adjective-placement.s: Put basic adjectives before nouns and after be to describe people and things.
ex: It is a **quiet** street.
My phone is **old**.
They live in a small **flat**.
She has **blue** eyes.

a1-simple-connectors.s: Use basic connectors to join short ideas in one sentence.
ex: I work in town **and** my sister studies online.
He wants to go, **but** he is too busy.
Would you like tea **or** coffee?
We took a taxi **because** it was late.

a2-past-simple-regular.s: Use the past simple to talk about finished actions in the past with regular verbs.
ex: I **visited** my aunt on Sunday.
They **played** tennis after school.
We **watched** a documentary last night.
She **studied** in the library yesterday.

a2-past-simple-irregular.s: Use common irregular past forms to talk about finished past events.
ex: I **went** to bed late last night.
She **saw** a fox in the garden yesterday.
We **had** lunch near the river.
He **made** dinner for everyone.

a2-past-simple-negatives-questions.s: Use did and didn't to make past simple negatives and questions.
ex: I **didn't** cook dinner yesterday.
**Did** you see the update?
Where **did** they meet?
She **didn't** like the hotel.

a2-past-continuous.s: Use the past continuous for actions in progress at a past time or around another past event.
ex: I **was reading** when the lights went out.
They **were waiting** outside at 7.
What **were you doing** at midnight?
He **wasn't listening** during the meeting.

a2-used-to.s: Use used to for past habits and states that were true before but are not true now.
ex: I **used to** have very long hair.
**Did** you **use to** live in Ankara?
He **didn't use to** eat spicy food.
My dad **used to** work nights.
a2-used-to.mw: I am used to wake early

a2-present-continuous-now-temporary.s: Use the present continuous for actions happening now and temporary situations around now.
ex: I **am waiting** for the bus.
She **is working** from home this week.
We **are getting** busier these days.
Why **are you laughing**?

a2-present-continuous-future-arrangement.s: Use the present continuous for fixed personal plans and arrangements in the near future.
ex: I **am having** lunch with my manager tomorrow.
She **is seeing** the dentist on Monday.
What **are you doing** after class?
They **are coming** over for dinner tonight.

a2-be-going-to.s: Use be going to for intentions and predictions based on present evidence.
ex: I **am going to buy** a new phone next month.
She **is going to study** medicine.
**Are you going to cook** tonight?
They **aren't going to move** this year.

a2-will-predictions-decisions.s: Use will for predictions, offers, promises, and decisions made at the moment of speaking.
ex: I think the test **will** be difficult.
Don't worry. I'll **help** you with the report.
The phone is ringing. I'll **get** it.
She **won't** forget your birthday.

a2-comparative-adjectives.s: Use comparative adjectives to compare two people, things, or situations.
ex: My brother is **taller** than me.
Today is **much colder** than yesterday.
Her new phone is **better** than mine.
The test was **easier** than I expected.

a2-superlative-adjectives.s: Use superlative adjectives to say which thing is the highest, lowest, best, or worst in a group.
ex: This is **the most useful** app on my phone.
It was **the best** meal of the weekend.
He is **the tallest** player on the team.
That was **the worst** film I saw all year.

a2-adverbs-of-frequency.s: Use adverbs of frequency to say how often something happens.
ex: I **usually** have tea after lunch.
She is **often** tired after work.
We **sometimes** go hiking at weekends.
He **never** drinks coffee.

a2-adverbs-of-manner.s: Use adverbs of manner to describe how someone does an action.
ex: She spoke very **quietly** during the meeting.
He drives **carefully** in bad weather.
The children waited **patiently** by the door.
My uncle cooks **well**.

a2-quantifiers-basic.t: Quantifiers: Much, Many, A Lot Of, A Few, A Little
a2-quantifiers-basic.s: Use basic quantifiers to talk about amount and number.
ex: There aren't **many** buses after 10.
We don't have **much** time left.
She drinks **a lot of** coffee.
I bought **a few** things for dinner.

a2-countable-vs-uncountable.s: Know which nouns can be counted and which are treated as amounts or substances.
ex: I need a **glass** and a **plate**.
We bought some **bread** and **cheese**.
She gave me two useful **tips**.
There isn't much **traffic** today.

a2-possessive-s.s: Use apostrophe s to show that something belongs to a person, animal, or group.
ex: That is my **brother's** bike.
We are at my **parents'** house.
The **children's** room is upstairs.
I borrowed the **teacher's** marker.

a2-subject-vs-object-questions-intro.s: Start to distinguish questions about the subject from questions about the object.
ex: **Who** called you last night?
**Who** did you call after work?
**What** happened at the meeting?
**What** did she buy?

a2-modals-must-mustnt-have-to.s: Use these forms to express obligation, necessity, and prohibition.
ex: You **must** show your ticket at the door.
I **have to** finish this report today.
Passengers **mustn't** smoke here.
She **has to** wear glasses for reading.

a2-modals-should-shouldnt.s: Use should and shouldn't to give advice and recommendations.
ex: You **should** drink more water.
He **shouldn't** spend so much on clothes.
**Should** I call the hotel first?
You **should** try the soup here.

a2-modals-could-would-basic.s: Use could for polite possibility or past ability, and would for polite requests and imagined situations.
ex: **Could** you help me with this form?
When I was ten, I **could** ride a horse.
It **could** rain later, so take a jacket.
**Would** you like a seat by the window?

a2-prepositions-of-movement.s: Use movement prepositions to show direction from one place to another.
ex: We walked **through** the park after lunch.
The cat jumped **onto** the table.
He cycled **across** the bridge in the rain.
Go **along** this road and turn left.

a2-verb-ing-vs-to-intro.s: Learn that some verbs are followed by -ing and others by to + verb.
ex: I enjoy **reading** on the train.
She wants **to study** engineering.
We finished **tidying** the kitchen.
He needs **to speak** to his teacher.

a2-so-because.s: Use because to give a reason and so to show a result.
ex: She stayed at home **because** she felt ill.
He was late, **so** he missed the start of the meeting.
I didn't cook **because** I got home very late.
They were hungry, **so** they ordered pizza.
a2-so-because.mw: I stayed in so I was tired
a2-so-because.mr: I stayed in **because** I was tired

a2-reflexive-pronouns.s: Use reflexive pronouns when the subject and object are the same, and in some common emphatic phrases.
ex: I taught **myself** some basic Italian.
She hurt **herself** while she was skiing.
We made the decorations **ourselves**.
Please help **yourself** to some coffee.

b1-present-perfect-simple-experience.s: Use the present perfect to talk about life experiences when the exact time is not important.
ex: Have you **ever stayed** in a capsule hotel?
We've **visited** that museum before.
He has **worked** with several small startups.
They've **been** to Lisbon twice.

b1-present-perfect-simple-unfinished-tim.s: Use the present perfect for actions and states in a time period that is still connected to now.
ex: I've **sent** six emails this morning.
She's **worked** from home all week.
We've **had** a lot of rain this month.
Have you **eaten** anything today?

b1-present-perfect-vs-past-simple.s: Choose between the present perfect and the past simple based on whether the time is finished or still connected to now.
ex: They **went** to Prague last summer.
Have you **ever eaten** Ethiopian food?
We've **already booked** the tickets.
He **didn't answer** my message yesterday.

b1-for-since-yet-already-just.t: For, Since, Yet, Already, and Just
b1-for-since-yet-already-just.s: Use these common time markers with the present perfect to show duration, expectation, completion, and recency.
ex: We've known each other **for** ten years.
She's lived in this street **since** 2019.
Have you finished the form **yet**?
I haven't eaten **yet**.

b1-past-perfect-simple.s: Use the past perfect to show that one past action happened before another past action or time.
ex: By the time we got there, the shop **had closed**.
She'd **already eaten** when I offered dinner.
I was nervous because I'd **never flown** before.
Had they **finished** the report before the meeting?

b1-zero-conditional.s: Use the zero conditional for general truths, facts, and results that always happen under the same condition.
ex: If you **mix** blue and yellow, you get green.
When I **drink** coffee late, I don't sleep well.
If people **don't water** these plants, they die quickly.
If the shop **is** closed, we go next door.
b1-zero-conditional.mw: If it rains, we stayed inside

b1-first-conditional.s: Use the first conditional for real and possible future situations and their likely results.
ex: I'll cook dinner **if you buy** the vegetables.
**If it rains** tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
What will you do **if he says** no?
**If my manager agrees**, I'll take Friday off.
b1-first-conditional.mw: If it will rain, we'll stay in

b1-second-conditional.s: Use the second conditional for unreal, unlikely, or imagined present and future situations.
ex: **If I had** a car, I'd drive to work.
I'd buy a bigger desk **if I had** the space.
**If I were** you, I'd speak to him today.
They'd travel more **if flights were** cheaper.
b1-second-conditional.mw: If I was you, I'd wait

b1-reported-speech-statements.s: Report what someone said without repeating the exact words, often with backshift.
ex: Mina **said she was feeling** tired.
He **told me he had** a meeting at 3.
They **said they'd call** later.
The teacher **said the test was** on Friday.

b1-passive-present-simple.s: Use the present simple passive when the action or process matters more than the person who does it.
ex: Rice **is grown** in this region.
The museum **is closed** on Mondays.
Breakfast **is served** from 7 to 10.
These products **are made** in Turkey.

b1-passive-past-simple.s: Use the past simple passive for actions done in the past when the result or receiver is more important than the doer.
ex: The old theatre **was renovated** last year.
The decision **was announced** on Monday.
My bike **was stolen** outside the station.
The bridge **was damaged** in the storm.

b1-modals-of-deduction-present.s: Use must, might, and can't to make logical guesses about a present situation.
ex: You've been working all day. You **must be** tired.
She isn't answering. She **might be** in a meeting.
They **might need** more time to finish.
This **must be** your umbrella.

b1-modal-obligation-have-to-must-need-to.t: Have To, Must, and Need To
b1-modal-obligation-have-to-must-need-to.s: Compare these forms to talk about obligation and necessity more precisely.
ex: I **have to** catch the last train home.
She **needs to** update her passport soon.
Do we **have to** pay in cash?
He **has to** finish the form today.

b1-defining-relative-clauses.s: Use who, which, and that to identify exactly which person or thing you mean.
ex: This is the book **that** everyone recommends.
I know a teacher **who** speaks four languages.
The app **that** we use at work just updated.
She wants a flat **which** has a balcony.
b1-defining-relative-clauses.mw: The woman which called is my aunt
b1-defining-relative-clauses.mr: The woman **who** called is my aunt

b1-gerund-vs-infinitive-verb-ing.s: Use common verbs that are followed by the -ing form after another verb.
ex: I enjoy **reading** before bed.
She avoided **answering** the question directly.
We finished **cleaning** the flat at noon.
He suggested **meeting** outside the station.

b1-gerund-vs-infinitive-verb-to.s: Use common verbs that are followed by to + base verb after another verb.
ex: I want **to buy** a better desk.
They decided **to stay** another night.
She hopes **to find** a job nearby.
We plan **to visit** my uncle in July.

b1-phrasal-verbs-introduction.s: Learn common everyday phrasal verbs and their basic meanings in context.
ex: Can you **turn on** the heater?
She's **looking for** her passport.
We **found out** that the train was cancelled.
He **gave up** smoking last year.

b1-so-such-too-enough.s: Use these forms to show degree, emphasis, excess, and sufficiency.
ex: The soup was **so** hot that I couldn't eat it.
It was **such** a noisy cafe that we left early.
This jacket is **too** small for me now.
Are you old **enough** to drive here?
b1-so-such-too-enough.mw: The room is too much small

b1-quantifiers-advanced.t: Advanced Quantifiers: Most, All, None, Both, Either, Neither
b1-quantifiers-advanced.s: Use these quantifiers to talk about totality, absence, and choice more precisely.
ex: **All** the information is in the email.
**Both** options look good to me.
You can sit on **either** side of the table.
**Neither** of my brothers drives.

b1-as-as-not-as-as.s: Use these patterns to compare equal and unequal degree.
ex: My new phone is **as** light **as** my old one.
The hotel wasn't **as** quiet **as** we'd hoped.
He runs **as** quickly **as** his brother.
This chair isn't **as** comfortable **as** that one.
b1-as-as-not-as-as.mw: This bag is as heavier as mine

b1-articles-zero-article-generic-the.t: Articles: Zero Article and Generic The
b1-articles-zero-article-generic-the.s: Use no article or the to talk about things in general in the right way.
ex: **Books** can be expensive in city-centre shops.
**Fresh air** usually helps me think clearly.
**Children** learn languages quickly.
**Technology** changes fast.

b1-used-to-vs-would-past-habits.t: Used To vs Would for Past Habits
b1-used-to-vs-would-past-habits.s: Compare used to and would when talking about repeated actions in the past.
ex: I **used to** be very shy at school.
When we were children, we **would** spend hours outside.
My uncle **used to** own a small bookshop.
I **used to** cycle to work before I moved.

b1-future-plans-contrast.t: Future Plans: Will, Going To, and Present Continuous
b1-future-plans-contrast.s: Choose the most natural future form for intentions, arrangements, predictions, and instant decisions.
ex: The phone is ringing. **I'll** answer it.
We're **going to** move in August.
**I'm having** lunch with the director tomorrow.
Look at those clouds. **It's going to** storm.

b1-question-forms-subject-vs-object.t: Question Forms: Subject vs Object Questions
b1-question-forms-subject-vs-object.s: Control subject and object question patterns more confidently across present and past simple forms.
ex: **Who** called you last night?
**Who** did you call after the meeting?
**What** happened to your phone?
**What** did they decide in the end?

b1-adverbs-of-degree-quite-rather-fairly.t: Adverbs of Degree: Quite, Rather, and Fairly
b1-adverbs-of-degree-quite-rather-fairly.s: Use these words to soften, strengthen, or nuance descriptions more naturally.
ex: That was **rather** a long meeting.
She's **quite** good at explaining things.
He answered **quite** calmly under pressure.
The road is **fairly** busy at this time of day.

b1-time-clauses.t: Time Clauses (when, while, as soon as, until, before, after)
b1-time-clauses.s: Use time clauses to connect actions in sequence and show when one event happens in relation to another.
ex: Call me **when** you leave the office.
I read the emails **while** I was waiting for the bus.
**After** I spoke to her, I felt much better.
**Before** you send the file, check the name.
b1-time-clauses.mw: I'll call you when I will arrive

b2-present-perfect-continuous.s: Use the present perfect continuous to focus on duration or repeated activity leading up to now.
ex: I **have been working** on this report since 8.
She **has been feeling** under pressure lately.
**Have** you **been sleeping** well recently?
He **has been running**, so he needs some water.

b2-past-perfect-continuous.s: Use the past perfect continuous to show an ongoing earlier-past activity before another past point.
ex: We **had been walking** for hours before we found the village.
She **had been studying** all afternoon, so she took a break.
They **had been arguing**, and the room felt tense.
**Had** you **been waiting** long when the doctor finally saw you?
b2-past-perfect-continuous.mw: He had been wait for an hour
b2-past-perfect-continuous.mr: He **had been waiting** for an hour

b2-third-conditional.s: Use the third conditional to imagine a different past and its possible past result.
ex: If **we had booked** earlier, **we would have saved** money.
**She would have called** you **if she had known**.
If **I hadnt forgotten** my charger, **my phone wouldnt have died**.
**If you had told** me, **I could have helped**.
b2-third-conditional.mw: If I would have known, I would have come
b2-third-conditional.mr: **If I had known**, **I would have come**

b2-mixed-conditionals.s: Use mixed conditionals to connect an unreal past condition with a present result, or less often the reverse.
ex: If I **had listened** to your advice, I wouldnt be in this mess now.
She would feel more confident now if she **had accepted** the role.
If he **were** more careful, he wouldnt have broken the screen.
We wouldnt be so tired now if we **had gone** to bed earlier.
b2-mixed-conditionals.mw: We wouldnt be late now if we left earlier
b2-mixed-conditionals.mr: We wouldnt be late now if we **had left** earlier

b2-wish-if-only-present-past.t: Wish and If Only: Present and Past
b2-wish-if-only-present-past.s: Use wish and if only to express regret, dissatisfaction, or a strong desire for a different present or past.
ex: I wish I **had** more free time during the week.
If only we **lived** nearer the station.
She wishes she **hadnt sold** her bike.
I wish I **were** better at small talk.
b2-wish-if-only-present-past.mw: I wish I know the answer

b2-modals-of-deduction-past.t: Modals of Deduction in the Past
b2-modals-of-deduction-past.s: Use must have, might have, and cant have to make logical guesses about past situations.
ex: The roads are wet, so it **must have rained** last night.
She isnt answering; she **might have left** her phone at home.
They **must have been** tired after the drive.
We **might have met** before, but Im not sure.

b2-modal-perfect-should-could-would-have.t: Modal Perfect: Should Have, Could Have, Would Have
b2-modal-perfect-should-could-would-have.s: Use modal perfect forms for regret, criticism, missed possibility, and unreal past results.
ex: You **should have told** me you were running late.
I **would have come**, but I was ill.
He **shouldnt have spoken** to her like that.
We **could have asked** for a refund.

b2-passive-across-tenses.s: Use passive forms in continuous and perfect tenses when the receiver of the action is more important than the doer.
ex: The main hall **is being cleaned** at the moment.
The windows **were being washed** when the alarm went off.
The final version **has been approved** by the client.
Our booking **had been confirmed** before we travelled.

b2-causative-have-get-something-done.s: Use have or get something done when someone else performs a service or task for you.
ex: I **had my phone screen replaced** last week.
She **got her hair cut** before the wedding.
Were **having the kitchen painted** next month.
He **had his passport renewed** before the trip.

b2-reported-speech-questions.s: Report yes/no and wh- questions without keeping direct question word order.
ex: She asked **if I had finished** the report.
He asked **where we were staying**.
My manager asked **why I had left** early.
She asked me **what I was doing** that weekend.

b2-reported-speech-commands-requests.s: Report orders, instructions, requests, and advice with the right verb pattern.
ex: She asked **us to come** a bit earlier.
He reminded **me to lock** the back door.
The guide told **us not to take** photos inside.
I asked **him to send** the address again.

b2-reporting-verbs-patterns.s: Use a wider range of reporting verbs with the correct grammar patterns.
ex: She admitted **making** a mistake in the budget.
He denied **taking** the keys.
They suggested **meeting** after lunch.
She accused **him of hiding** the truth.

b2-non-defining-relative-clauses.s: Use non-defining relative clauses to add extra, non-essential information about a person or thing.
ex: My sister, **who works in finance**, loves hiking.
The museum, **which closes at 5**, is free on Tuesdays.
Our car, **which we bought second-hand**, has been very reliable.
Leo, **whose flat is near the station**, walks to work.
b2-non-defining-relative-clauses.mw: Leo, which lives near us, cycles to work
b2-non-defining-relative-clauses.mr: Leo, **who lives near us**, cycles to work

b2-reduced-relative-clauses.s: Shorten some relative clauses to make sentences more compact and natural.
ex: The man **waiting by the lift** is our new designer.
The package **delivered this morning** is for you.
Passengers **travelling with children** can board first.
People **working remotely** need secure access.
b2-reduced-relative-clauses.mw: The people waited outside are cold

b2-linking-contrast.s: Use a wider range of contrast linkers to compare, qualify, and balance ideas.
ex: **Although** the food was excellent, the service was slow.
**Despite** the traffic, we arrived on time.
**In spite of** feeling ill, he went to work.
**Despite** the delay, the audience stayed calm.
b2-linking-contrast.mw: My sister likes tea whereas I coffee
b2-linking-contrast.mr: My sister likes tea, **whereas** I prefer coffee

b2-linking-result-purpose.t: Linking Words of Result and Purpose
b2-linking-result-purpose.s: Use varied structures to express purpose and consequence more precisely.
ex: I wrote the address down **so that** I wouldnt forget it.
We reduced the font size **in order to** fit everything on one page.
The roads were blocked; **therefore**, the bus took a different route.
He saved his work frequently **so that** he wouldnt lose anything.
b2-linking-result-purpose.mw: I left early so that catch the train
b2-linking-result-purpose.mr: I left early **so that** I could catch the train

b2-future-perfect.s: Use the future perfect to show that something will be completed before a future time or event.
ex: By the end of the week, well **have completed** the redesign.
She **will have arrived** by the time the meeting starts.
I **wont have saved** enough money by August.
**Will they have finished** the repairs before winter?
b2-future-perfect.mw: They will have been leave by 8

b2-future-continuous.s: Use the future continuous for actions that will be in progress at a particular time in the future.
ex: This time tomorrow, Ill **be flying** over the Alps.
**Will you be joining** us for lunch?
Dont call at 3; Ill **be presenting** then.
**Will the team be using** this room after 2?

b2-articles-advanced-patterns.s: Use articles more accurately with geography, institutions, and common fixed expressions.
ex: We crossed **the Danube** by train.
We met at **the cinema** after work.
He studied medicine at **university**.
They stayed at **home** because it was snowing.

b2-determiners-each-every-all-whole.t: Determiners: Each, Every, All, and Whole
b2-determiners-each-every-all-whole.s: Choose the right determiner to talk about individuals, total groups, and complete units.
ex: **Every** room in the hotel has a balcony.
**All** the guests had arrived by 8.
I spent the **whole** morning answering emails.
**Each** of the answers was different.

b2-inversion-intro-never-rarely-seldom.s: Use inversion after words like never, rarely, and seldom for formal emphasis.
ex: **Seldom** has the office been this quiet.
**Never** did she apologise for the mistake.
**Rarely** are the roads empty at this hour.
**Seldom** do they stay open after midnight.

b2-participle-clauses-basic.s: Use participle clauses to make sentences shorter and show time, reason, or result more compactly.
ex: **Feeling** unwell, she cancelled the meeting.
**Shocked** by the price, we decided to wait.
He left the room without **saying** goodbye.
**Turning** the page, I saw my name at the top.

b2-adverb-placement-modifying-adverbs.s: Place adverbs more naturally and use modifiers to adjust meaning with greater precision.
ex: She **almost** forgot the tickets at home.
The room is **slightly** warmer than yesterday.
They have **probably** already left.
I **nearly** dropped my phone on the stairs.

b2-phrasal-verbs-separable-inseparable.s: Use a wider range of phrasal verbs and know when the object can or must move.
ex: Please turn it **off** before you leave.
The heating broke **down** again last night.
They set **up** the new system in two days.
Can you deal **with** this customer complaint?

c1-inversion-negative-adverbs-advanced.s: Use inversion after fronted negative or limiting expressions for formal emphasis and dramatic style.
ex: **Hardly** had I closed my laptop when the fire alarm started.
**Not until** the final page did I understand the title.
**Only then** did they admit the figures were wrong.
**Rarely** have I seen such a careful response.
c1-inversion-negative-adverbs-advanced.mw: Only then I realised the truth
c1-inversion-negative-adverbs-advanced.mr: **Only then** did I realise the truth

c1-cleft-sentences-it-cleft.s: Use it-clefts to highlight one part of a sentence and control emphasis more precisely.
ex: It **was** Nina who suggested the new layout.
It **is** the price that worries me most.
It **was** on Tuesday that we finally heard back.
It **was** Alex who noticed the error first.
c1-cleft-sentences-it-cleft.mw: It was James sent the file
c1-cleft-sentences-it-cleft.mr: It **was** James who sent the file

c1-cleft-sentences-what-cleft-all-cleft.s: Use what-clefts and all-clefts to focus on actions, needs, or key information in a sentence.
ex: **What** I need right now is a break from email.
**All** she wanted was a quiet evening at home.
**What** matters is that we respond quickly.
**All** I can say is that we tried our best.
c1-cleft-sentences-what-cleft-all-cleft.mw: All I want are a refund

c1-unreal-conditionals-without-if.s: Use should you, were you to, and had you to form formal unreal or tentative conditionals without if.
ex: **Should** you require any assistance, let me know.
**Were** you to accept the offer, you would start in June.
**Had** they checked the figures, they would have noticed the error.
**Should** the printer fail again, call the support desk.
c1-unreal-conditionals-without-if.mw: Should you needed help, ask me

c1-subjunctive-formal-that-clauses.s: Use the subjunctive base form in formal that-clauses after verbs and adjectives of recommendation, necessity, or urgency.
ex: The doctor recommended that he **reduce** his working hours.
It is vital that every applicant **bring** photo ID.
She insisted that the figures **be** checked again.
We suggested that the launch **wait** until Monday.
c1-subjunctive-formal-that-clauses.mw: She suggested that he goes later

c1-advanced-modality.s: Use advanced modal combinations to express nuanced certainty, likelihood, necessity, and future obligation.
ex: This may well be the **last chance** we get this year.
If the budget changes, **wed have to** postpone the launch.
You might just **catch the earlier** train if you leave now.
**Theyll have to** hire more staff if orders keep rising.

c1-discourse-markers-formal.s: Use formal discourse markers to organise argument, contrast viewpoints, and guide the listener or reader through complex reasoning.
ex: The software is cheaper; **moreover**, it integrates well with our existing tools.
The road was crowded. **Nonetheless**, we arrived on time.
The data were incomplete; **consequently**, the review was postponed.
Our first option is faster. **On the other hand**, the second is less risky.
c1-discourse-markers-formal.mw: Furthermore the roads were blocked but we arrived early
c1-discourse-markers-formal.mr: The roads were blocked. **Nonetheless**, we arrived early

c1-hedging-and-softening.s: Use hedging language to sound less absolute, more tactful, and more academically or professionally appropriate.
ex: **It seems that** the market has stabilised for now.
The opening section is **somewhat** unclear and may need revision.
**Apparently**, the update has already been rolled out.
This approach **tends to** work better with smaller groups.
c1-hedging-and-softening.mr: This **appears to be** inaccurate / This **may not be** correct

c1-emphasis-do-fronting.s: Use emphatic do and fronting to strengthen a statement or focus attention on key information.
ex: I **do** understand why they were frustrated.
**That detail**, I had completely forgotten.
**The risk**, however, we cannot ignore.
What I **do** object to is the timing.
c1-emphasis-do-fronting.mw: The timing, I dont like it

c1-ellipsis-and-substitution.s: Use ellipsis and substitution to avoid repetition and make speech and writing more natural and efficient.
ex: I wanted the **red** one, not the **green** one.
She said she would help, **and she did**.
Do you think it will work? I think **so**.
Mine is faster, but **theirs isnt**.

c1-advanced-passive-reporting.s: Use reporting passives such as it is said that and he is said to to present information impersonally and formally.
ex: It **is widely believed** that the results were influenced by timing.
The minister **is said to be** considering a resignation.
The building **is thought to have been** damaged in the storm.
The actor **is believed to have** moved abroad.

c1-advanced-reported-speech-patterns.s: Use advanced reporting verbs and tense handling to report denial, accusation, suggestion, and stance with precision.
ex: He **denied changing** the deadline without approval.
She **accused the supplier of misleading** the team.
They **insisted that** the original wording be kept.
They **warned us that** delays were likely.

c1-participle-clauses-perfect-passive.s: Use perfect and passive participle clauses to show earlier time, cause, and compressed background information.
ex: **Having reviewed** the draft, I could see exactly where the problem was.
**Having been warned** about the traffic, we left before dawn.
**Having finished** lunch, they returned to the workshop.
**Having been overlooked** for years, the archive is finally being digitised.
c1-participle-clauses-perfect-passive.mw: Having saw the message, I replied

c1-relative-clauses-advanced.s: Use whose, of which, and preposition + relative pronoun patterns for more precise and formal reference.
ex: The company, **whose** profits fell sharply, announced a restructuring plan.
The device, **without which** the test cannot be completed, is extremely fragile.
The committee, **several members of which** opposed the change, delayed the vote.
The colleague **with whom** I shared the project has moved abroad.
c1-relative-clauses-advanced.mw: The proposal to that everyone objected was withdrawn
c1-relative-clauses-advanced.mr: The proposal **to which** everyone objected was withdrawn

c1-future-in-the-past.s: Use forms such as would, was going to, and was about to to talk about future meaning from a past viewpoint.
ex: I didnt realise that the conversation **would change** everything.
We **were going to stay** another night, but the hotel was full.
She **was about to send** the email when the system crashed.
He said the team **would arrive** by noon.

c1-verb-patterns-object-infinitive-gerun.s: Use advanced verb patterns such as verb + object + infinitive and verb + object + ing where needed.
ex: The coach encouraged the team **to stay** calm under pressure.
She reminded me **to attach** the final file.
I caught him **reading** my notes.
We found the children **playing** in the garden.

c1-determiners-no-not-any-any-every-scar.t: Determiners and Quantifiers: No, Not Any, Any, Every, Scarcely Any
c1-determiners-no-not-any-any-every-scar.s: Use these forms more precisely to express absence, free choice, universality, and very limited quantity.
ex: There was **no** reason to delay the decision.
We couldnt find **any** reliable evidence.
You can choose **any** seat in the back row.
**Every** detail in the contract matters here.

c1-articles-idiomatic-zero-patterns.s: Use articles accurately in idiomatic expressions and advanced zero-article patterns.
ex: He went to **bed** straight after the flight.
Shes still at **work**, so call later.
We travelled by **train** and returned by **coach**.
She was in **charge** of the whole event.

c1-punctuation-for-meaning.s: Use commas, semicolons, and dashes to shape meaning, pace, and clarity in complex sentences.
ex: The proposal, **which had already been revised twice**, was still unclear.
The weather had improved; **however**, the roads were still unsafe.
We met in Paris, France; **Porto**, Portugal; and Ghent, Belgium.
The test was long, **but** fair.
c1-punctuation-for-meaning.mw: My sister who lives in Milan is visiting
c1-punctuation-for-meaning.mr: My sister, **who lives in Milan**, is visiting if the information is extra

c1-complex-subordination-linking.s: Use layered subordination to build precise complex sentences while keeping time, cause, concession, and condition relationships clear.
ex: **Although** the original timeline was too short, we continued **because** the client had already announced the date.
**If** the servers fail again **when** traffic peaks, the platform could become unstable.
The report, **which** was completed under pressure, still reads clearly **because** the structure is strong.
**Since** the team had already tested the backup, they were confident, **even though** the rollout remained risky.
c1-complex-subordination-linking.mw: Although because the data were late, we postponed the meeting
c1-complex-subordination-linking.mr: **Because** the data were late, we postponed the meeting / **Although** the data were late, we continued
